Helpers may aid the breeding pair in raising young (Brackbill 1970b, Tarbell 1983). At one nest, the helper was one of the previous year's offspring of the adult female and a different male (Brackbill 1970b). In another case, the helper was the offspring of the breeding pair from a previous season (Tarbell 1983). Such helping behavior is unusual for parids and has only been reported in two other species, Bridled Titmice (Baeolophus wollweberi; Nocedal and Ficken 1998a) and Black Tits (Parus niger; Brown 1987). There is no information on whether helping affects breeding success of the adult pair.

Females only incubate and brood the young, but both males and females bring food to the nestlings. Group members help during nesting. During nest building, group members only follow the nest building female around the territory, although Willis (1961) observed one non-reproductive individual carrying material to the nest. Helpers contribute with nest defense and feeding nestlings; helpers start feeding nestlings on day 5 after hatching and, on average, they make 4.5% (18 of the 397) of the total feeding trips (Willis 1961).

Nests often attract the attention of extra adults that associate with a pair for up to an entire breeding season; these extra birds are sometimes tolerated and occasionally lead to polygyny (217). In New York, extra birds were predominantly males (219, 325), whereas in Washington, extra birds were yearling females (217). Extra adults contribute relatively little to feeding young, but they are known to mob predators and assist in nest-building, incubation, and brooding young (219, 325, 217). Extra adults may be using nest attendance as a breeding strategy either to replace one pair member should something happen to it (217) or to commit sexually selected infanticide (219, 325), providing an opportunity for males to take over the breeding female (see Behavior: Sexual Behavior). Nests that are attended by helpers often are ones occupied by older females (325), consistent with the interpretation that male attendants are trying to secure high-quality females as mates.

Trios (1 male, 2 females) have been reported in Great Lakes colonies; all three birds incubated eggs, and brooded and fed offspring (Shugart 1980). Trios comprised about 0.8% of nesting associations at colonies in northeastern Lake Michigan in 1978-81 (Fitch and Shugart 1983), but have not been reported elsewhere. Birds in trios usually remained together in successive years. Trios had lower hatching success and lower productivity than male-female pairs

Not known to occur, although young of first brood often remain on natal territory after nestlings from second brood have hatched. In rare cases siblings, returning as yearlings, establish territories adjacent to each other but no cooperative behavior, despite evidence of kin recognition (Wheelwright and Mauck 1998, Wheelwright et al. 2006).

Not observed. Fledglings from one brood sometimes remain on territory when parents rear a second brood. No observations of young helping at the later nest. In cases when first-year birds return to establish territories near their natal territory, no observations of cooperative behavior between these birds and their older relatives. Neighboring males that share song themes do not cooperate (in contrast, they countersing and chase each other), yet song activity in neighborhoods may attract other males and females to mate.

Although ca. 20% of Canada Jay pairs studied in Quebec and Ontario have an associated nonbreeder on their territories at the onset of breeding and ca. 65% of these are the pair's own offspring from the previous breeding season, the nonbreeders do not feed the current year's nestlings and the breeders energetically drive them away if they approach the nest. Starting immediately after the nestlings fledge, however, adults relax this vigilance and on intensively observed territories in Ontario and Quebec some non-breeders have accounted for over 30% of all observed feedings of the young (189, 190). Proposed explanation for this pattern holds that, compared to other jays, Canada Jays are particularly vulnerable to nest predators because they have poorer defensive abilities (being smaller and generally having only one extra group member, if any). In such a species, suppression of allofeeding, along with a smaller than expected clutch size and a very low provisioning rate by the adults (achieved by bringing largest possible loads at the consequently minimum possible frequency), may reduce predator-attracting visits to the nest and thus contribute to higher breeding success (166, 191). In contrast to Western Bluebirds, Eastern Bluebirds rarely have helpers. In joint nesting, 2 females lay 2 clutches of eggs synchronously in the same nest, then incubate synchronously and sequentially, and cooperate with a male in feeding nestlings and fledglings. In S. Carolina, 5 of 4,299 nesting attempts in field seasons 1977–1991 were joint nesting ventures; 2 of these 5 attempts were by the same previously known and banded females, so it was reliably inferred that these jointly-nesting females were mother and daughter (PAG, JHP). Juvenile helpers are rare; almost all reports are of juveniles entering nesting cavities when adults are feeding later broods (Pinkowski 1975d)—something documented on video films twice by PAG and JHP. Adult helpers seen occasionally and irregularly (Pinkowski 1976d, PAG), usually second-year son of current breeders.

Cooperative breeding is apparently rare (< 0.1%), but is likely to be under-reported because it requires detailed observation. Several male-female-female trios were detected at Bermuda in a period when the sex ratio was strongly female-biased (see Behavior: Mating System and Sex Ratio). One male-male-female trio has been reported in Germany (Ludwigs 2004). Otherwise, cooperative breeding has not been investigated at the sites where supernormal clutches are most frequent (see Eggs: Clutch Size, above).

True helping does not occur in this species (Lombardo 1986b): investigatory visits may have been misinterpreted as helping (e.g. Wetherbee 1933). Rarely, apparent “helping” behavior may result when multiple females attempt to breed in same box (Rendell 1992). Only one confirmed case (by RRC) in which two males were delivering food to the same nestlings.

Fledglings have been observed helping build nests (Tarwater 2006). This appears to be more beneficial for offspring in terms of learning rather than helping parents. The fledglings collected nest material and in some cases they put the nesting material on the nest (but did not actually weave the material into the nest) and in other cases they dropped the nesting material while trying to fly with it. Older fledglings, which have developed the ability to sing, will help defend the natal territory with their parents (Tarwater 2006).

Extremely rare if not absent in most temperate populations. One report from California of a juvenile from a first brood helping its father (and possibly mother; she was unmarked) feed young of a second brood in the same season (275. Second report from Kansas of a juvenile of unknown origin feeding young and removing a fecal sac from a nest at least one time (Timson and Farley 2003). Helpers-at-the-nest also reported in Costa Rica, but not in all nests and such behavior was apparently rare (Skutch 1940, 176, Skutch 1983, Winnett-Murray 1986). Skutch (1983) speculated helping was more likely when young from a previous brood sleep with the mother in the nest while she incubates in a subsequent breeding attempt. In one case in Costa Rica, an individual known not to be the offspring of a resident parents' previous brood attempted to feed young; parents repeatedly attacked that individual (Winnett-Murray 1986: 23).

Does not occur (17, MTM). Trios of adults occasionally form, but are rarely stable; a trio in New York remained together from early in nestling period to > 1 mo after young had fledged (MTM). The fate of the third bird in next year was determined in 2 of 3 cases in which the third bird was banded and sex determined. In one case, a female returned to breed on territory where she was seen in previous year (former male and female occupants of territory failed to return). In the other case, a male established residence on adjacent territory in following year. Third birds in trios probably represent birds prospecting for a breeding site in the next year.
